content: The needs of the population must be addressed, and fostering ownership of the plan is essential. Since most stakeholders will be involved in implementing the National Strategic Plan (NSP), it is critical to ensure they fully understand and contribute to its development. Adapting the NSP at subnational levels is vital because the implementation of interventions primarily occurs at community and facility levels. Given the heterogeneity of populations, geographical variations, infrastructure differences, local health financing mechanisms, and the burden and determinants of tuberculosis (TB), these variations must be considered to adapt the national plan effectively at subnational levels. The subnational planning process depends on the degree of decentralization within the health governance system. Lessons learned from the implementation of previous plans can also inform the administrative levels of the health system that should participate in the planning process. Promoting quality care that is effective, safe, and people-centered is a priority. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes quality care across the health system. The principles, pillars, and components of the End TB Strategy include government stewardship and accountability with monitoring and evaluation (M&E), strong coalitions with civil society organizations and communities, protection and promotion of human rights, ethics, and equity, and adaptation of the strategy and targets at the country level with global collaboration. The pillars and components of the End TB Strategy include: 1. Integrated, patient-centered care and prevention: Early diagnosis of TB, including universal drug susceptibility testing (DST), and systematic screening of contacts and high-risk groups. Treatment of all TB cases, including drug-resistant TB, with patient support. Collaborative TB/HIV activities and management of comorbidities. Preventive treatment for high-risk individuals and vaccination against TB. 2. Bold policies and supportive systems: Political commitment with adequate resources for TB care and prevention. Engagement of communities, civil society organizations, and public and private care providers. Universal health coverage (UHC) policies and regulatory frameworks for case notification, vital registration, quality and rational use of medicines, and infection control. Social protection, poverty alleviation, and addressing other determinants of TB. 3. Intensified research and innovation: Discovery, development, and rapid uptake of new tools, interventions, and strategies. Research to optimize implementation and impact while promoting innovations. The WHO Multisectoral Accountability Framework to End TB (MAF-TB) aims to accelerate progress toward ending TB by strengthening the TB response beyond the health sector and ensuring accountability among governments and stakeholders at global, regional, and country levels. Civil society, TB-affected communities, and patient groups play a fundamental role in adapting and implementing this framework. The framework includes four components: national commitments, actions taken on those commitments, monitoring and reporting approaches, and progress on high-level multisectoral collaboration and review mechanisms. The MAF-TB cycle, launched in 2019, outlines the framework's components, elements, and principles. It includes checklists and annexes to help countries assess the status of their TB response and the accountability of ministries and governmental bodies. These assessments should involve government ministries, local governments, civil society, TB-affected communities, parliamentarians, the private sector, public-private partnerships, philanthropic organizations, professional associations, research institutes, and universities. Information generated through MAF-TB baseline assessments should contribute to the NSP's situation analysis. Based on these assessments, countries can design interventions to strengthen the framework's components according to their national constitutional, legal, or regulatory frameworks and other relevant factors. These interventions should be reflected in the NSP. The process for developing a TB NSP involves six phases: 1. Planning and preparation: Establishing a core organizing team. Developing a detailed roadmap for the NSP development process. Mobilizing and confirming resources for strategic planning. 2. Conducting the situation analysis: Reviewing TB epidemiology and determinants. Conducting a TB program review and consolidating data and evidence. Synthesizing the situation analysis with stakeholder input. 3. Developing the NSP components: Setting goals, objectives, and strategic interventions. Outlining activities and subactivities. Including contingency measures for service disruptions. Establishing monitoring and evaluation metrics. 4. Developing metrics and activities for monitoring, evaluation, and review: Formulating indicators and targets for activities and subactivities. Outlining monitoring and evaluation activities. 5. Costing: Producing cost estimates. Identifying projected funding and sources. 6. Consensus, endorsement, dissemination, and resource mobilization: Achieving consensus and endorsement of the NSP. Disseminating the plan and advocating for its implementation. Mobilizing resources to support the plan. The indicative timeline for the entire process is 6–12 months, though this may vary. The roadmap for NSP development should outline key timelines, milestones, and resource needs, including financial and technical expertise. It should also identify stakeholders who may require preliminary sensitization, especially those from sectors beyond health. The roadmap should be endorsed by relevant Ministry of Health (MOH) offices and existing bodies for multisectoral coordination of the TB response. The situation analysis should systematically collect and study information to inform the NSP's development. It should cover all pillars and components of the End TB Strategy, identifying key gaps across relevant sectors. At a minimum, it should include an epidemiological review of TB, a review of social determinants of TB, a TB program review, and a consolidation of data and evidence. The epidemiological review provides background information on the TB burden and epidemic characteristics in the country, as well as an overview of the TB surveillance system. It assesses the level and trends of TB burden and evaluates the surveillance system's capacity to measure TB burden and its distribution across the population. A standardized checklist should be used to assess data quality, system coverage, TB mortality, and surveillance of TB, including drug-resistant TB and relevant comorbidities. Stakeholder mapping and engagement are critical to the strategic planning process. Stakeholders include individuals or groups affected by, influencing, or interested in the strategic plan. Mapping involves identifying key stakeholders relevant to the country's TB response.
